reference.source: Goldfrank's Toxicologic Emergencies / Mandell's Principles and Practice of Infectious Diseases
clinicalPearls: An infusion-rate-related reaction to vancomycin causing flushing, erythema and pruritus over the face, neck and upper trunk
It is a non-immune (anaphylactoid) reaction driven by direct mast-cell degranulation, not a true IgE-mediated allergy
Onset is typically during or shortly after a rapid infusion, and it often eases when the infusion is slowed or paused
More severe episodes can include hypotension, chest and back pain, and muscle spasm
Prevention centres on slowing the infusion rate; antihistamine pre-treatment can reduce or blunt the reaction
Distinguishing it from true anaphylaxis is important, as the reaction does not necessarily contraindicate future vancomycin use with a slower infusion
Other agents that provoke histamine release (for example certain opioids or muscle relaxants) can potentiate the reaction
The presence of urticaria beyond the infusion, angio-oedema or bronchospasm should raise concern for true allergic anaphylaxis
reference.pathophysiology: The reaction results from direct, non-immunological degranulation of mast cells and basophils provoked by vancomycin, releasing histamine into the circulation. Because it does not require prior sensitisation or drug-specific IgE, it can occur on first exposure and is closely related to the rate and concentration of the infusion, with rapid administration causing a larger histamine surge. Histamine produces cutaneous vasodilatation and flushing, pruritus and, when release is marked, hypotension and muscle discomfort. This anaphylactoid mechanism contrasts with true type I hypersensitivity, in which drug-specific IgE cross-links mast-cell receptors; the distinction guides whether the drug can be cautiously continued at a slower rate.
additionalDifferentials: True IgE-mediated anaphylaxis to vancomycin or a co-administered drug
Systemic hypersensitivity or DRESS from vancomycin (linear IgA disease with vancomycin is a separate entity)
additionalInvestigations: Clinical observation of the temporal relationship to infusion rate
Vital sign monitoring for hypotension during infusion
Serum tryptase where true anaphylaxis needs to be excluded
Assessment for urticaria, angio-oedema or bronchospasm suggesting true allergy
Trial of slowed infusion with observation under supervision
redFlags: Significant hypotension or cardiovascular instability during infusion
Angio-oedema, bronchospasm or stridor suggesting true anaphylaxis
Widespread urticaria persisting after the infusion
Chest pain or severe muscle spasm
reference.prognosis: The reaction is usually mild and self-limiting once the infusion is slowed or stopped, and vancomycin can often be continued with a slower infusion and antihistamine cover. Severe hypotensive episodes are uncommon but require prompt supportive treatment.
pitfalls: Mislabelling the reaction as a true penicillin-class-style allergy and permanently avoiding an effective antibiotic
Failing to slow the infusion and instead abandoning treatment unnecessarily
Missing genuine anaphylaxis by assuming all vancomycin flushing is benign
Overlooking co-administered histamine-releasing drugs that potentiate the reaction
references: Mandell, Douglas, and Bennett's Principles and Practice of Infectious Diseases
management: Stop or slow the vancomycin infusion at symptom onset, then recommence at a slower rate once the reaction settles
Prevent recurrence by extending the infusion duration for subsequent doses
Give antihistamine premedication with an H1 blocker, with or without an H2 blocker, to blunt the histamine-mediated reaction
Provide supportive treatment with intravenous fluids for hypotension in severe episodes
Distinguish the reaction from true IgE-mediated anaphylaxis using serum tryptase and features such as urticaria, angio-oedema or bronchospasm, since it does not contraindicate future cautious use
Review and minimise co-administered histamine-releasing drugs, and consider an alternative glycopeptide only if reactions persist despite rate reduction
